opus-5.5.text:
Well, it really comes down to what we think intelligence actually is and where it has to live. The Alberta Plan is built around the idea of an agent that's continually interacting with a world that's vastly bigger and more complex than the agent itself. That's the situation every natural intelligence finds itself in, and it's the situation any useful machine intelligence will find itself in too. The world isn't going to slow down and wait for you to finish your computation.

So if you take that seriously, computational efficiency stops being a nice engineering detail and becomes central to the science. An agent has a finite budget of computation and memory at every moment. It has to perceive, predict, plan, and learn, all in real time, while the stream of experience keeps coming. If your learning algorithm only works when you can store everything and replay it endlessly, or when you have a data center behind every decision, then you haven't really solved the problem of how a mind learns from experience. You've solved a different, easier problem.

There's also the lesson Rich Sutton has talked about a lot, the bitter lesson: the methods that win out in the long run are the ones that scale with computation. But scaling with computation isn't the same as wasting computation. We want methods whose performance keeps improving as you give them more resources, and that means the per-step cost of learning and acting really matters. Things like incremental, online updates, linear-time algorithms, methods that can learn continually without catastrophically forgetting, those are the building blocks we need.

And personally, coming from my work with prosthetic limbs and assistive technologies, this is very concrete for me. When you've got a learning system running on a small device attached to someone's body, adapting to them moment by moment, you can't send everything off to the cloud and wait. The system has to learn on the fly, with limited hardware, and it has to be reliable. That experience really reinforces the idea that efficient, continual learning isn't a constraint we tolerate; it's the heart of what makes an intelligent agent actually useful in the real world.

r001.rationale: The response says agents have finite compute and that per-step cost matters, but it does not clearly explain that efficiency enables more learning from a given amount of computation.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, it comes down to the simple fact that an agent in the real world doesn't get to pause time. That's really the heart of it. If you're an agent interacting with a stream of experience, data is arriving continually, and you have to make a decision now, with whatever computation you have available right now. You can't say to the world, "Hold on, let me go think about this for a few hours and get back to you." The world keeps moving.

So in the Alberta Plan, we put a lot of emphasis on what we call the computational budget, or the idea that an agent's learning and decision-making should scale linearly, or close to it, with the amount of computation it has per time step. The methods we're interested in are ones that are online, incremental, and whose cost per step doesn't grow as the agent accumulates more experience. If every new piece of data makes the next update more expensive, you've built something that eventually grinds to a halt. That's not a viable design for an intelligence that's supposed to keep learning over a lifetime.

There's a deeper reason too, and it's one Rich Sutton has articulated very well in "The Bitter Lesson." The methods that have won out historically are the ones that make the best use of available computation, and computation keeps getting cheaper. So if you design your agent around methods that scale gracefully with compute, you ride that wave. If you design it around clever hand-built structure that doesn't scale, you get left behind. We want methods where, when you give them ten times more compute, they get meaningfully better, not methods that plateau.

And I'd add one thing from my own background, working with people who use prosthetic limbs. There you feel this very concretely. The device has to adapt to the person, in real time, on hardware that fits in a socket on someone's arm. There is no cloud to go and ask. The learning has to happen there, continually, and cheaply. That experience really drove home for me that computational efficiency isn't a nice-to-have, it's what makes continual learning possible at all.

r001.rationale: The response says efficient methods make the best use of available computation and allow an agent to keep learning within a fixed per-step computational budget.

astra-6.text:
Computational efficiency matters because an intelligent agent has to learn and act with finite resources. It has a limited amount of computation, a limited amount of memory, and a limited amount of time to make a decision. Meanwhile, the world keeps moving.

In the Alberta Plan, we take those constraints seriously from the beginning. The question is how an agent can keep learning from an ongoing stream of experience while making good use of the computation available to it. If learning becomes more and more expensive as experience accumulates, that’s a problem for an agent we want to learn throughout its lifetime.

Think about an artificial limb interacting with a person. It needs to respond when the person needs it, and it needs to adapt as they use it. Computational efficiency is part of making that intelligence useful in the moment. It’s a fundamental part of the problem we’re trying to solve.

r001.rationale: The response says the agent must learn from ongoing experience while making good use of available computation, and explains that rising learning costs would hinder lifelong learning. This communicates that efficiency allows more learning within finite computational resources.

sol-6.1.text:
Because an agent has to learn and act with the resources it actually has. It has a finite amount of computation, a finite amount of memory, and a limited amount of time to respond. Those constraints aren’t incidental to intelligence; they help define the problem we’re trying to solve.

In the Alberta Plan, we’re interested in agents that learn continually through interaction. The world doesn’t pause while they do an expensive calculation. If an agent takes too long to update its predictions or choose an action, it can miss the opportunity to do something useful.

So computational efficiency is about making learning practical at every step. We want an agent to get more capable through experience while remaining able to operate within its resource budget. That’s particularly tangible in robotics, where a system needs to respond as events unfold.

r001.rationale: The response says agents must learn within a resource budget, but does not clearly state that efficiency enables more learning from a given amount of computation.
